Thomson (August 5, 1877 – July 8, 1917) was a Canadian artist active in the early 20th century. During his short career, he produced roughly 400 oil sketches on small wood panels and approximately 50 larger works on canvas. [ note 4 ] His works consist almost entirely of landscapes , depicting trees, skies, lakes, and rivers. He used broad brush strokes and a liberal application of paint to capture the beauty and colour of the Ontario landscape. Thomson is considered by many Canadians as the archetypal painter, [ 6 ] and his later work has heavily influenced Canadian art – paintings such as The Jack Pine and The West Wind have taken a prominent place in the culture of Canada and are some of the country's most iconic works. His accidental death by drowning at 39 shortly before the founding of the Group of Seven is seen as a tragedy for Canadian art. Canadian art. Raised in rural Ontario, Thomson was born into a large family of farmers and displayed no immediate artistic talent. He worked several jobs before attending a business college, eventually developing skills in penmanship and copperplate writing. At the turn of the 20th century, he was employed in Seattle and Toronto as a pen artist at several different photoengraving firms, including Grip Ltd. There he met those who eventually formed the Group of Seven, including J. E. H. MacDonald , Lawren Harris , Frederick Varley , Franklin Carmichael and Arthur Lismer . In May 1912, he visited Algonquin Park —a major public park and forest reservation in Central Ontario —for the first time. It was there that he acquired his first sketching equipment and, following MacDonald's advice, began to capture nature scenes. He became enraptured with the area and repeatedly returned, typically spending his winters in Toronto and the rest of the year in the Park. His earliest paintings were not

the area and repeatedly returned, typically spending his winters in Toronto and the rest of the year in the Park. His earliest paintings were not outstanding technically, but showed a good grasp of composition and colour handling. His later paintings vary in composition and contain vivid colours and thickly applied paint. Thomson developed a reputation during his lifetime as a veritable outdoorsman , talented in both fishing and canoeing , although his skills in the latter have been contested. The circumstances of his drowning on Canoe Lake in Algonquin Park, linked with his image as a master canoeist, led to unsubstantiated but persistent rumours that he had been murdered or committed suicide. Although he died before the formal establishment of the Group of Seven, Thomson is often considered an unofficial member. Life [ edit ] Early years [ edit ] Thomas John Thomson was born on August 5, 1877, in Claremont, Ontario (and lived briefly on the farm belonging to his grandfather Thomas “Tam” Thomson on 8th Concession after immigrating from Aberdeenshire, Scotland), [ 8 ] the sixth of John and Margaret Thomson's ten children. [ 9 ] He was raised in Leith (on Concession A), [ 10 ] Ontario, near Owen Sound , in the municipality of Meaford . [ 11 ] Thomson and his siblings enjoyed both drawing and painting, although he did not immediately display any major talents. [ 9 ] He was eventually taken out of school for a year because of ill health, including a respiratory problem variously described as "weak lungs" or "inflammatory rheumatism ". [ 11 ] [

[ 11 ] [ 12 ] This gave him free time to explore the woods near his home and develop an appreciation of nature. [ 9 ] The family were unsuccessful as farmers; both Thomson and his father often abandoned their chores to go hiking, hunting and fishing. [ 13 ] Thomson regularly went on walks in Toronto with Dr. William Brodie (1831–1909) , his grandmother's first cousin. [ 14 ] [ 15 ] Brodie was a well-known entomologist , ornithologist and botanist , and Thomson's sister Margaret later recounted that they collected specimens on long walks together. [ 16 ] [ 17 ] Thomson was also enthusiastic about sports, once breaking his toe while playing football. [ 11 ] He was an excellent swimmer and fisherman, inheriting his passion for the latter from his grandfather and father. [ 18 ] Like most of those in his community, he regularly attended church. [ 11 ] In 1901, Thomson enrolled at Canada Business College in Chatham , Ontario. The school advertised instruction in stenography , bookkeeping , business correspondence and "plain and ornamental penmanship ". [ 18 ] There, he developed abilities in penmanship and copperplate —necessary skills for a clerk. [ 22 ] After graduating at the end of 1901, he travelled briefly to Winnipeg before leaving for Seattle in January 1902, joining his older brother, George Thomson. [ 18 ] [ 22 ] [ 19 ] George and cousin F. R. McLaren had established the Acme Business School in Seattle, listed as the 11th largest business school in the United States. [ 20 ] Graphic design work [ edit ] Seattle (1901–1904) [ edit ] After studying at the business school for six months, Thomson was hired at Maring & Ladd as a pen artist, draftsman and etcher . [ 18 ] [ 22 ] [ 24 ] He mainly produced business cards, brochures and posters, as well as three-colour printing . [ 22 ] [ 24 ] Having previously learned calligraphy , he specialized in lettering, drawing and painting. [ 24 ] While working at Maring & Ladd, he was known to be stubbornly independent; his brother Fraser wrote that, instead of completing his work according to the direction provided, he would use his own design ideas, which angered his boss. [ 25 ] Thomson may have also worked as a freelance commercial designer, but there are no extant examples of such work. [ 26 ] He eventually moved on to a local engraving company. Despite a

a freelance commercial designer, but there are no extant examples of such work. [ 26 ] He eventually moved on to a local engraving company. Despite a good salary he left by the end of 1904. He quickly returned to Leith, possibly prompted by a rejected marriage proposal after his brief summer romance with Alice Elinor Lambert . [ 27 ] [ 24 ] Lambert, who never married, later became a writer; [ 28 ] in one of her stories, she describes a young girl who refuses an artist's proposal and later regrets her decision. During this time, Thomson was known to dress well and spend his money on nice clothes and fine dining. Thomson moved to Toronto in the summer of 1905. He was enamoured with the Park, and many of his works were painted in the area. Algonquin Park was established in 1893 by Oliver Mowat and the Ontario Legislature . Covering eighteen rectangular townships in Central Ontario , the Park was created to provide a space dedicated to recreation, wildlife and watershed protection,

[ 50 ] Thomson learned of the Park from fellow artist Tom McLean. [ 51 ] [ 52 ] In May 1912, aged 34, he first visited the Park, venturing through the area on a canoe trip with his Grip colleague H. B. (Ben) Jackson. [ 53 ] Together, they took the Grand Trunk Railway from Toronto to Scotia Junction, then transferred to the Ottawa, Arnprior and Parry Sound Railway , arriving at Canoe Lake Station. [ 52 ] McLean introduced Thomson to the Park superintendent, G. W. Barlett. [ 51 ] [ 54 ] Thomson and Jackson later met ranger Harry (Bud) Callighen while they camped nearby on Smoke Lake. [ 51 ] [ 55 ] It was also at this time that Thomson acquired his first sketching equipment. [ 51 ] [ 56 ] He did not yet take painting seriously. first sketching equipment. [ 51 ] [ 56 ] He did not yet take painting seriously. According to Jackson, Thomson did not think "his work would ever be taken seriously; in fact, he used to chuckle over the idea". [ 57 ] Instead, they spent most of their time fishing, [ 57 ] except for "a few notes, skylines and colour effects". [ 51 ] During the same trip, Thomson read Izaak Walton 's 1653 fishing guide The Compleat Angler . [ 58 ] Primarily a fisherman's bible, the book also provided a philosophy of how to live, similar to the one described in Henry David Thoreau 's 1854 book Walden, or Life in the Woods , a reflection on simple living in natural surroundings. [ 58 ] His time in Algonquin Park gave him an ideal setting to imitate Walton's "contemplative" life. [ 59 ] Ben Jackson wrote: Tom was never understood by lots of people, was very quiet, modest and, as a friend of mine spoke of him, a gentle soul. He cared nothing for social life, but with one or two companions on a sketching and

He cared nothing for social life, but with one or two companions on a sketching and fishing trip with his pipe and Hudson Bay tobacco going, he was a delightful companion. If a party or the boys got a little loud or rough Tom would get his sketching kit and wander off alone. At times he liked to be that way, wanted to be by himself commune [ sic ] with nature. [ 59 ] Upon returning to Toronto, Jackson published an article about his and Thomson's experience in the Park in the Toronto Sunday World , included in which were several illustrations. [ 51 ] After this initial experience, Thomson and another colleague, William Broadhead, went on a two-month expedition, going up the Spanish River and into Mississagi Forest Reserve (today Mississagi Provincial Park ). [ 60 ] [ 61 ] Much of his artwork from this trip, mainly oil sketches and photographs, was lost during two canoe spills; [ 60 ] the first was on Green Lake in a rain squall and the second in a series of rapids. [ 62 ] [ note 6 ] In fall 1912, Albert Robson, Grip's art director, moved to the design firm Rous & Mann. [ 3 ] A month after returning to Toronto, Thomson followed Robson and left Grip to join Rous & Mann too. [ 50 ] [ 43 ] [ 64 ] They were soon joined by Varley, Carmichael and Lismer. [ 62 ] Robson later spoke favourably of Thomson's loyalty, calling him "a most diligent, reliable and capable craftsman". [ 39 ] Robson's success in attracting great talent was well understood. [ 65 ] Employee Leonard Rossell believed that the key to Robson's success "was that the artists felt that he was interested in them personally and did all he could to further their progress. [ 62 ] A frequent visitor to the Ontario Society of Artists ' (OSA) exhibitions, MacCallum was admitted to the Arts and Letters Club in January 1912. There, he met artists such as John William Beatty , Arthur Heming , MacDonald and Harris. [ 62 ] MacCallum eventually persuaded Thomson to leave Rous and Mann and start a painting career. [ 67 ] MacCallum recognized Thomson's and Jackson's talents and offered to cover their expenses for one year if they committed themselves to painting full time. [ 68 ] [ 69 ] MacCallum and Jackson both encouraged Thomson to "take up painting seriously, [but] he showed no enthusiasm. The chances of earning a livelihood by it did not appear to him promising. He was sensitive and independent, and feared he might become an object of patronage." [ 67 ] MacCallum wrote that when he first saw Thomson's sketches, he recognized their "truthfulness, their feeling and their sympathy with the grim fascinating northland ... they made me feel that the North had gripped Thomson as it had gripped me since I was eleven when I first sailed and paddled through its silent places." He described Thomson's paintings as "dark, muddy in colour, tight and not wanting in technical defects". [ 70 ] After Thomson's death, MacCallum helped preserve and advocated for his work. [ 69 ] Thomson accepted MacCallum's offer under the same terms offered to Jackson. [ 67 ] He travelled around Ontario with his colleagues, especially to the wilderness of Ontario, which was to become a major source of inspiration. Regarding Algonquin Park, he wrote in a letter to MacCallum: "The best I can do does not do the place much justice in the way of beauty." [ 71 ] He ventured to rural areas near Toronto and tried to capture the surrounding nature. He may have worked as a fire ranger on the Mattagami reserve . [ 75 ] Thomson became as familiar with logging scenes as with nature in the Park and painted them both. [ 76 ] While returning to Toronto in November 1912, Thomson stopped in Huntsville . [ 75 ] [ 77 ] The visit was possibly to meet with Winifred Trainor, a woman whose family owned a cottage on Canoe Lake in Algonquin Park. Trainor was later rumoured to have been engaged to Thomson with a wedding planned for the late 1917, although little is known about their relationship. Jackson recalled that in the fall of 1914, Thomson threw his sketch box into the woods out of frustration, [ 83 ] and was "so shy he could hardly be induced to show his sketches". [ 46 ] Harris expressed similar sentiments, writing that Thomson "had no opinion of his own work", and would even throw burnt matches at his paintings. [ 84 ] Several of the canvases he sent to exhibitions remained unsigned. [ note 8 ] If someone praised one of his sketches, he immediately gave it to them as a gift. [ 46 ] A turning point in his career came in 1914, when the National Gallery of Canada , under the directorship of Eric Brown, began to acquire his paintings. Although the money was not enough to live on, the recognition was unheard of for an unknown artist. [ 86 ] For several years he shared a studio and living quarters with fellow artists, initially living in the Studio Building with Jackson in January 1914. Jackson described the Studio Building as "a lively centre for new ideas, experiments,

living in the Studio Building with Jackson in January 1914. Jackson described the Studio Building as "a lively centre for new ideas, experiments, discussions, plans for the future and visions of an art inspired by the Canadian countryside". [ 87 ] It was there that Thomson, "after much self-deprecation, finally submitted to becoming a full-time artist". [ 88 ] They split the rent—$22 a month—on the ground floor while construction on the rest of the building was finished. [ 31 ] After Jackson moved out in December to go to Montreal , Carmichael took his place. [ 31 ] [ 89 ] [ 90 ] Thomson and Carmichael shared a studio space through the winter. [ 91 ] On March 3, 1914, Thomson was nominated as a member of the OSA by Lismer and T. G. Greene. He was elected on the 17th. He did not participate in any of their activities beyond sending paintings for annual exhibitions. [ 46 ] Harris described Thomson's strange working hours years later: When he was in Toronto, Tom rarely left the shack in the daytime and then only when it was absolutely necessary. He took his exercise at night. He would put on his snowshoes and tramp the length of the Rosedale ravine and out into the country, and return before dawn. [ 92 ] Thomson with his catch at Canoe Lake , Algonquin Park , c. 1915 In late April 1914, Thomson arrived in Algonquin Park, where he was joined by Lismer on May 9. They camped on Molly's Island in Smoke Lake, travelling to Canoe, Smoke, Ragged, Crown and Wolf Lakes. [ 93 ] He spent his spring and summer divided between Georgian Bay and Algonquin Park, visiting James MacCallum by canoe. His travels during this time have proved difficult to discern, with such a large amount of ground covered in such a short time, painting the French River , Byng Inlet , Parry Sound and Go-Home Bay from May 24 through August 10. Though World War I had erupted that year, he and Jackson went on a canoe trip, in October meeting up with Varley and his wife Maud, as well as Lismer and his wife Esther, and daughter Marjorie. [ 101 ] This marked the first time three Group of Seven members painted together, and the only time they worked with Thomson. [ 61 ] [ 86 ] In his 1958 autobiography, A Painter's Country , A. Y. Jackson wrote that, "Had it not been for the war, the Group [of Seven] would have formed several years earlier and it would have included Thomson." [ 103 ] Why Thomson did not serve in the war has been debated. [ 104 ] Mark Robinson and Thomson's family said that he was turned down after multiple attempts to enlist, likely due to his poor health and age but also possibly

Robinson and Thomson's family said that he was turned down after multiple attempts to enlist, likely due to his poor health and age but also possibly because he had flat feet . [ 11 ] [ 21 ] [ 86 ] Blodwen Davies wrote that Thomson's artist friends tried to convince him to not risk his life, but he decided to secretly volunteer anyway. [ 105 ] Andrew Hunter has found this scenario to be improbable, especially given that other artist friends did volunteer for the war, such as A. Y. Jackson. [ 104 ] Thomson's sister suggested that he was a pacifist and that "he hated war and said simply in 1914 that he never would kill anyone but would like to help in a hospital, if accepted". [ 106 ] William Colgate wrote that Thomson "brooded much upon" the war and that "he himself did not enlist. Rumour has it that he tried, and failed to pass the doctor. This is doubtful." McMichael Canadian Art Collection, Kleinburg With MacCallum's year of financial support over, Thomson's financial future became uncertain. [ 90 ] He briefly looked into applying for a position as a park ranger, but balked after seeing that it could take months for the application to go through. Instead, he considered working in an engraving shop over the winter. [ 149 ] His upturned canoe was spotted later in the afternoon, and his body was discovered in the lake eight days later. [ 60 ] [ 61 ] His first trips to Algonquin Park inspired him to follow the lead of fellow artists in producing oil sketches of natural scenes on small, rectangular panels for easy portability while travelling. David Silcox has described these paintings as "the visual equivalent of a national anthem, for they have come to represent the spirit of the whole country, notwithstanding the fact that vast tracts of Canada have no pine trees", [ 180 ] and as "so majestic and memorable that nearly everyone knows them". [ 181 ] Arthur Lismer described them similarly, saying that the tree in The West Wind was a symbol of the Canadian character, unyielding to the wind and emblematic of steadfastness and resolution. [ 182 ] Thomson had a great enthusiasm for trees and worked to capture their forms, their surrounding locations, and the effect of the seasons on them. [ 7 ] In 2004, another historical marker honouring Thomson was moved from its previous location near the centre of Leith to the graveyard in which he is now buried. [ 248 ] Though best known for his painting, Thomson is often mythologized as a veritable outdoorsman . James MacCallum contributed stories to this image.
